transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Well, hello Doctor. It’s nice to meet you. You know, it’s a bit funny that I’m even here at my age. I'm seventy years old, completely retired, and you'd think I'd just be sitting in my armchair enjoying the quiet, but my daughter—she’s actually the one who suggested I come talk to you—she says I just never seem to stop. And I suppose when I really sit down and think about it, she has a point. 

I just feel like I’m always up and moving around the house. Constantly in motion. Like, take yesterday for example, which was supposed to be just a nice, quiet Tuesday with absolutely nothing on the calendar. I started out sitting at the kitchen table looking at the sign-up list for my garden club—we're doing a spring bulb sale, you see, and I volunteered to organize the tulip orders—but before I even got halfway down the page, I was up and digging through my knitting bag in the living room because I suddenly remembered a pattern I wanted to check for my grandson's sweater. But did I actually start knitting? No, because while I was looking for the yarn, I saw the travel papers for that bus trip to Branson I'm supposed to be taking next month, and I started sorting through those on the coffee table! 

I’m just bouncing from the garden club list to my knitting bag to the travel papers, all day long, before I’ve really finished any one thing I started. It’s like I have this motor inside me that just keeps me pacing and puttering from room to room. My late husband used to say I was like a hummingbird, bless his heart, but lately it just feels a little exhausting to never just sit and rest.
Did you have this same kind of restlessness and difficulty staying on one task when you were a child?

Oh, my goodness, yes. It’s funny you ask that because I was just thinking about my old elementary school—Oak Street Elementary, which they tore down years ago to build a pharmacy, such a shame—but anyway, yes, this goes way, way back. 

I remember my mother, Lord rest her soul, she used to come back from those parent-teacher conferences just shaking her head and sighing. Even back in grade school, my teachers told my mother the exact same thing every single year. They’d tell her I was a very bright girl, but just completely scattered. I mean, I was always losing my papers. My spelling homework, my arithmetic sheets, permission slips... they would just vanish into thin air, or we'd find them weeks later crumpled up at the bottom of my bookbag under a mashed sandwich. 

And the talking! Oh, I was always talking out of turn. I just had so many thoughts popping into my head and I couldn't seem to hold them in, so I'd just blurt things out right in the middle of a lesson or turn around to tell my neighbor a story. And I could never just sit still to get my tasks done. Those old wooden desks they had back in the fifties were so hard and uncomfortable anyway, but I was always wiggling in my seat, twisting this way and that, trying to get up before I had even finished my work. My third-grade teacher, Mrs. Higgins—she always wore these thick glasses and smelled like peppermint—she actually moved my desk right up next to the chalkboard because I was just constantly squirming and chatting when I was supposed to be focusing on my penmanship. 

So, yes, I suppose this motor of mine has been running for a very, very long time. Back then, of course, they didn't really make a fuss about it, they just called you a chatterbox or a fidgeter and told you to try harder to sit still. But it's just always been how I am, you know? Even my brothers used to tease me because I couldn't just sit and watch a television program with them without getting up to fiddle with the antenna or go look out the window...
Have you noticed any new problems with your memory lately?

Well, memory... you know, that’s a funny thing to bring up, because at my age, everyone always assumes if you forget something, it’s just because you’re getting older. And I suppose that’s true to some extent, but honestly, I feel like my memory has always been a bit like a sieve. But to answer your question about lately... well, yes, I suppose things do slip my mind quite a bit. 

Just the other day—oh, it must have been Thursday, because Thursday is when the mail carrier, Tom, usually drops off the circulars—I meant to call my friend Betty back. She had left a message about our church bake sale, and I thought to myself, "I'll just call her back right after I finish sorting these coupons." But then, of course, I started looking at the coupons, and I saw a deal on those little cocktail wieners my daughter likes, which made me think about what I needed to pick up for supper. So I thought, "I should go to the store and get those, and maybe some of that nice crusty bread..." 

But did I write it down? No. Did I call Betty? No. I completely forgot about both things until my daughter came over later that evening and asked what we were having for supper! And then, just last week, I had an appointment to get my hair set at the salon down the street—Sylvia’s, she’s been doing my hair for fifteen years—and I meant to write the time on the calendar in the kitchen. But I got distracted wiping down the counter, and the appointment just completely slipped away from me until Sylvia actually called the house to ask where I was! 

So, yes, it happens all the time. I’ll mean to call someone back, or pick up something specific for supper, or write down an appointment, and then poof! It just vanishes from my head until someone else brings it up. It’s terribly embarrassing, really, especially when I have to apologize to Sylvia for keeping her waiting...
Before age 12, did you have these same attention and restlessness problems?

Well, yes, absolutely. I know I was just talking about Oak Street Elementary a moment ago, but it really is true—it started way back then, before I was even twelve years old. 

Like I mentioned, my mother would come home from those parent-teacher conferences just exhausted with me. Every single year, from first grade right on through, the teachers would say, "She’s a bright girl, but she’s just so scattered!" And they were right, I really was. I was constantly losing my assignments. My spelling lists, the math worksheets, those little permission slips they’d hand out for field trips—I’d lose them all. They’d just disappear, or end up crumpled into a little ball at the very bottom of my school bag underneath a crushed apple. 

And the wiggling! Oh, I just could not sit still in those hard wooden desks. I’d be twisting and turning, practically jumping out of my seat before I’d even finished my lessons. And I was always, always talking out of turn. A thought would just pop into my head, and I couldn't hold it back, so I'd just blurt it right out in the middle of a lesson, or spin around in my chair to tell the girl behind me a story. So, yes, all of this—the restlessness, the scattered feeling—it was all right there when I was a little girl.
